summary: Clarifies and extends the Bootstrap Protocol. It tightens up the loosely defined behavior of BOOTP relay agents and of clients. It was replaced by RFC 1542.

plainLanguage.summary: The original instructions for a helper who passes messages along were vague. This memo spells out exactly what that helper and the client should do.

questions: how do bootp relay agents work
subtitle: Clearer rules for how BOOTP relay agents and clients should behave.

tldr.problem: The original BOOTP specification left important details unclear, especially how relay agents should forward messages between clients and servers on different networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC clarifies the behavior of relay agents, clients, and servers, and adds a BROADCAST flag to help clients receive replies when they cannot handle unicast delivery.
tldr.outcome: BOOTP implementations became more consistent and interoperable. This RFC was superseded by RFC 1542, which added further improvements.

today: RFC 1542 superseded this RFC, providing additional improvements to BOOTP relay agent and client behavior. Modern systems typically use DHCP instead of BOOTP, but DHCP extensions still follow these foundational clarifications.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP) is a UDP/IP protocol that lets a computer configure itself when it boots up. It can learn its IP address, the address of a boot server, the boot file to load, and other configuration like the subnet mask and default router addresses.

The original BOOTP specification left several important details unclear. This RFC clarifies the behavior of BOOTP relay agents (also called forwarding agents), which are intermediaries that relay BOOTREQUEST messages from clients to servers on different networks, and relay BOOTREPLY messages back. It also clarifies client and server behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: BOOTP helps new computers learn who they are and where to find their boot file. This memo fixes vague parts of the original instructions so everyone does it the same way.

sections.title: The BROADCAST Flag and Message Fields
sections.content:
This RFC formally defines the 'flags' field in BOOTP messages, which was previously designated as unused. The most significant bit of the 'flags' field is the BROADCAST flag.

When a BOOTP client cannot receive unicast IP datagrams (only broadcasts), it sets the BROADCAST flag to 1. This signals relay agents and servers to send BOOTREPLY messages as broadcasts instead of trying unicast delivery. The remaining bits of the 'flags' field are reserved for future use and must be set to zero by clients and ignored by servers.

The RFC also clarifies the use of other fields: the 'secs' field should measure elapsed time since the first BOOTREQUEST (in seconds), the 'ciaddr' field should contain the client's known IP address (or 0.0.0.0), and the 'giaddr' field (gateway address) is for relay agents only, not a router to be used by the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds a flag that lets a client say 'I can only hear broadcasts' so the server knows to broadcast the answer instead of sending it directly. It also clears up what the other address fields in the message are supposed to mean.

sections.title: Client Behavior and Special Networks
sections.content:
BOOTP clients MUST set the 'giaddr' field to zero in all BOOTREQUEST messages. Clients SHOULD NOT interpret the 'giaddr' field in BOOTREPLY messages as the IP address of a router; they should ignore it.

The RFC clarifies that if a client knows a previous IP address, it MAY include it in 'ciaddr', but if it does not know its address, it SHOULD set 'ciaddr' to 0.0.0.0. Clients SHOULD fill the 'vend' (vendor information) field with a four-octet magic cookie, typically 99.130.83.99, to help servers identify what vendor-specific format to use.

For clients on IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks, special handling is needed because of non-transparent bridging. Clients SHOULD send BOOTREQUEST messages with an All Routes Explorer RIF to let servers cache the return route. Servers SHOULD respond to the client's hardware address with a Spanning Tree Rooted RIF.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients should ignore the gateway address field and set their own gateway address field to zero. They can tell the server their old address if they remember it. On Token Ring networks, the handshake works slightly differently because bridges work differently.

sections.title: BOOTP Relay Agent Rules
sections.content:
BOOTP relay agents forward BOOTREQUEST messages from clients to servers and BOOTREPLY messages back to clients. They are distinct from IP routers: instead of transparently forwarding packets, they receive BOOTP messages as the final destination and generate new BOOTP messages.

A relay agent must have a configuration mechanism to enable or disable relaying (disabled by default). When a BOOTREQUEST arrives, the relay agent MAY use the 'secs' field value as a policy factor to decide whether to relay. If the 'giaddr' field is zero, the relay agent MUST fill it with the IP address of the receiving interface. If 'giaddr' is already non-zero, it MUST NOT be modified. The relay agent MUST increment the 'hops' field and preserve all other fields.

When sending the request to the server (or servers), the destination must be configurable, independent of other broadcast forwarder configurations. Crucially, all BOOTREQUEST messages from a given client MUST be relayed to the same destination(s) to avoid issues with multi-message protocols like DHCP.

For BOOTREPLY messages, the relay agent must verify that the 'giaddr' field matches one of its directly-connected interfaces. If it does, the relay agent examines the BROADCAST flag: if set, it broadcasts the reply; if clear, it unicasts to the 'yiaddr' field. The reply MUST have its UDP destination port set to BOOTPC (68).
sections.plainLanguage: Relay agents are the postal workers: they pick up BOOTREQUEST messages from clients and deliver them to servers, then pick up BOOTREPLY messages and deliver them back. They must not change the messages except to fill in which interface the request came from and add a hop count, and they must route replies based on the BROADCAST flag.

sections.title: Security and Server Delivery Strategy
sections.content:
The RFC notes that BOOTP has significant security weaknesses. Because BOOTP is built on UDP and IP which are inherently insecure, and configuration hosts may not have passwords or keys available, authentication between servers and clients is difficult. Unauthorized servers can send false information (wrong addresses, spoof routers, spoof nameservers), and malicious clients can masquerade as legitimate clients or claim all resources.

For servers delivering BOOTREPLY messages, the RFC specifies a precise strategy: first check the 'ciaddr' field and send unicast to that address if non-zero; if 'ciaddr' is zero, check 'giaddr' and send to that relay agent address if non-zero; if both are zero, examine the BROADCAST flag and either broadcast (if set) or unicast to 'yiaddr' (if clear).
sections.plainLanguage: BOOTP has security problems because messages are not authenticated. Anyone can pretend to be a BOOTP server and feed wrong information to computers. Servers need to be careful about how they send replies back, following specific rules based on the address fields.
